context: The integer n is positive. For k > 0, quadratic_recur(k) creates an array nums of length k and calls itself with k−1. The figure omits the final call quadratic_recur(0), which allocates no array. For simplicity it shows termination and return on the row for 1. The code actually returns immediately when its argument is 0.
description: From left to right the columns are “Length of nums,” “Descend,” and “Unwind.” A line connects each length to its call in the same row. A brace labeled “Recursion depth n” spans the n levels that allocate arrays. Ellipses stand for intermediate calls. An arrow labeled “Reach the base case” leads from the row for 1 to the right column, where upward arrows connect the return 0 steps.

frames.explanation: Each outer call keeps its local array while waiting for its child. At the bottom of the figure, the lengths sum to 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) + n = n(n+1)/2, with an arrow to quadratic space, O(n²). At maximum depth the code has one additional frame for argument 0, but that call allocates no array. The O(n) stack overhead does not change the O(n²) peak space determined by the arrays.
frames.title: Arrays retained across recursive calls use quadratic space

summary: Each recursive level retains a local array. To find peak space, add the lengths of the arrays in all calls that have yet to return.
